Reading map · Previous chapter · Next chapter
A complete renderer makes the forward graphics model executable from camera and geometry through light estimation. The chapter’s value is the end-to-end connection and the evidence it exposes.
By the end: Trace a renderer from scene inputs to image output and identify its evidence limits.
Recall question: Which components must agree for a rendered image to test the intended forward model?
A complete renderer makes the forward model executable

This lab is a small, original teaching implementation that joins camera geometry, ray intersections, visibility, Monte Carlo integration, and color output in one runnable Python script. It is an independent example; it is not course project code, a reconstruction of a student project, or a production renderer.
Run it with Python 3 and no installed packages:
The default run writes a 96 by 64 P6 PPM image to renderer-lab.ppm. FFmpeg can convert it to PNG for a quick preview:

The image has a black background because the renderer models no environment illumination. It shows two matte spheres above a matte plane, lit by a rectangular emitter. Shadows are computed by testing finite rays from each visible surface point to sampled points on the light. The script deliberately supports one surface interaction: a camera ray hits a surface, then that point receives direct illumination from the area light. It does not bounce light between objects, so it has no indirect fill, color bleeding, glass, or mirror reflections. A black shadow therefore means “no direct ray from this light reached the surface,” not “no light exists in a real room.”
For a larger, less jagged preview, run:
Chapter.Code: python3 renderer_lab.py --width 384 --height 256 --spp 8 --light-samples 16 --seed 178 --output renderer-lab-large.ppm ffmpeg -y -i renderer-lab-large.ppm renderer-lab-large.png
Chapter.Content: Camera and geometry

A camera ray starts at the pinhole and passes through a position on the image plane. The script builds an orthonormal camera frame from the camera position, look target, and world-up direction. The image-plane coordinates use aspect ratio and a 48-degree vertical field of view. Each pixel receives four jittered primary rays by default; averaging them is a simple supersampling strategy that softens jagged edges. A fixed random seed makes the run repeatable. Increasing --spp gives more camera samples per pixel, while --light-samples controls the number of area-light samples at each camera hit:

Spheres use the quadratic ray intersection. Since ray directions are normalized, the quadratic coefficient for is one, and the nearer root is normally the visible entry point. If the ray begins inside a sphere, that entry root is negative, so the code tries the farther positive exit root. The plane is the equation : a ray parallel to it has no intersection, otherwise its parameter is the vertical distance to the plane divided by the ray’s vertical direction. All accepted hits must have greater than a small positive threshold and less than the current nearest hit. Here is a distance in scene units because the ray direction has unit length.

The scene occupies roughly six units across, so EPS = 0.0001 is a small scale-relative offset. After a surface hit, the shadow-ray origin moves by EPS along the surface normal to avoid immediately intersecting the surface it just left. Keep two rays conceptually distinct: the lighting integral uses and from the true surface point , while visibility starts at the offset point . For that visibility segment, the code recomputes and its length, so the ray aims exactly at the sampled emitter point. The maximum segment parameter ends just before that point. An object behind the emitter must not shadow it. Too large an epsilon can detach shadows from contact points; too small an epsilon can cause numerical self-intersections. The startup assertions exercise the sphere exit root, nearest-hit ordering, an actual finite shadow segment, offset-to-target segment geometry, and linear-to-sRGB endpoint behavior.
Area-light estimate

The rectangular light is described by a center and two half-edge vectors. Its area is four times the area of the half-edge parallelogram. The cross product of those half-edges gives the emitter normal, which points down toward the scene. The sampler chooses two independent uniform values in and maps them across the rectangle. That is uniform area sampling with probability density ; it is not a solid-angle PDF.

For a Lambertian surface with RGB diffuse reflectance , the BRDF is . If is a surface point, a sampled point on the light, , , and is one when the segment is visible and zero when blocked, direct outgoing radiance is
The two cosines are clamped to zero when either surface faces away from the other. Replacing the integral with uniform area samples gives the estimator

The implementation accumulates each RGB channel separately. The factor converts the sample average back to an area integral; omitting it or treating as a solid-angle density would give the wrong scale. The inverse-square factor and both cosines arise from converting an emitting area element into the irradiance arriving at the receiving surface. Larger lights subtend a wider angle and usually create softer shadow boundaries, which these samples resolve as some points on the emitter are visible while others are occluded.
Color and display

The material reflectances are dimensionless RGB values between zero and one. Light radiance is stored as linear RGB values in common relative units; values are chosen for this demonstration and are not calibrated physical measurements. If the channels were calibrated radiometric bands, multiplying by dimensionless reflectance and the geometric integral would preserve radiance units. In either case, the code must do lighting and averaging in linear light: encoded display values are not proportional to energy.

After all camera samples for a pixel have been averaged, a fixed two-times exposure is applied, followed by a Reinhard curve to map nonnegative, unbounded radiance to display range. The result is encoded with the piecewise sRGB transfer function and rounded to 8-bit channel values. Tone mapping happens after averaging, because clipping or compressing each noisy sample first would bias the average. The output is a binary P6 PPM: an ASCII header followed by three bytes per pixel in row-major RGB order. It is intentionally easy to write and inspect.

This miniature leaves out many real-renderer concerns: indirect illumination, physically calibrated spectral color, texture filtering, acceleration structures, anti-aliasing beyond jitter, variance reduction, multiple importance sampling, adaptive sampling, denoising, and robust scale-independent intersection tolerances. It is useful precisely because the direct-light estimator and its geometry fit in one small file. Each assumption is visible, testable, and connected to the image it produces.

#!/usr/bin/env python3 """A deterministic, direct-lighting teaching renderer. Standard library only.""" import argparse import math import random PI = math.pi EPS = 1.0e-4 # Scene units; scene spans roughly six units.
def add(a, b): return (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1], a[2] + b[2]) def sub(a, b): return (a[0] - b[0], a[1] - b[1], a[2] - b[2]) def mul(a, s): return (a[0] * s, a[1] * s, a[2] * s) def dot(a, b): return a[0] * b[0] + a[1] * b[1] + a[2] * b[2] def cross(a, b): return (a[1]*b[2] - a[2]*b[1], a[2]*b[0] - a[0]*b[2], a[0]*b[1] - a[1]*b[0]) def length(a): return math.sqrt(dot(a, a)) def unit(a): n = length(a) if n == 0.0: raise ValueError("cannot normalize a zero vector") return mul(a, 1.0 / n)
# Sphere tuple: (center, radius, diffuse RGB reflectance). Plane is y=0. SPHERES = [ ((-0.68, 0.72, 0.05), 0.72, (0.78, 0.20, 0.10)), ((0.62, 0.48, -0.36), 0.48, (0.12, 0.38, 0.82)), ] FLOOR_ALBEDO = (0.62, 0.64, 0.67) LIGHT_CENTER = (0.0, 3.25, -0.10) LIGHT_HALF_U = (1.25, 0.0, 0.0) LIGHT_HALF_V = (0.0, 0.0, 0.90) LIGHT_NORMAL = unit(cross(LIGHT_HALF_U, LIGHT_HALF_V)) # Faces down. LIGHT_AREA = 4.0 * length(LIGHT_HALF_U) * length(LIGHT_HALF_V) LIGHT_RADIANCE = (5.5, 4.8, 4.0) # Linear RGB radiance, relative units.
def sphere_hit(origin, direction, sphere, t_max=float("inf")): center, radius, _ = sphere oc = sub(origin, center) half_b = dot(oc, direction) # Direction is normalized, so a=1. c = dot(oc, oc) - radius * radius disc = half_b * half_b - c if disc < 0.0: return None root = math.sqrt(disc) # Test the entry root, then the exit root: rays may start inside a sphere. for t in (-half_b - root, -half_b + root): if EPS < t < t_max: point = add(origin, mul(direction, t)) return (t, point, unit(sub(point, center)), sphere[2]) return None
def plane_hit(origin, direction, t_max=float("inf")): if abs(direction[1]) < 1.0e-10: return None # Parallel to y=0. t = -origin[1] / direction[1] if EPS < t < t_max: point = add(origin, mul(direction, t)) return (t, point, (0.0, 1.0, 0.0), FLOOR_ALBEDO) return None
def scene_hit(origin, direction, t_max=float("inf")): nearest = None for sphere in SPHERES: hit = sphere_hit(origin, direction, sphere, t_max) if hit and (nearest is None or hit[0] < nearest[0]): nearest = hit hit = plane_hit(origin, direction, t_max) if hit and (nearest is None or hit[0] < nearest[0]): nearest = hit return nearest
def occluded(origin, direction, distance): # A finite segment ends just before the sampled emitter point. return scene_hit(origin, direction, max(EPS, distance - 2.0 * EPS)) is not None
def sample_area_light(rng): # Uniform area PDF = 1/A: independent uniform coordinates on the rectangle. a, b = rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0), rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) return add(LIGHT_CENTER, add(mul(LIGHT_HALF_U, a), mul(LIGHT_HALF_V, b)))
def direct_radiance(point, normal, albedo, rng, light_samples): total = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] shadow_origin = add(point, mul(normal, EPS)) for _ in range(light_samples): light_point = sample_area_light(rng) delta = sub(light_point, point) distance2 = dot(delta, delta) distance = math.sqrt(distance2) wi = mul(delta, 1.0 / distance) cos_surface = max(0.0, dot(normal, wi)) cos_emitter = max(0.0, dot(LIGHT_NORMAL, mul(wi, -1.0))) if cos_surface == 0.0 or cos_emitter == 0.0: continue shadow_delta = sub(light_point, shadow_origin) shadow_distance = length(shadow_delta) shadow_direction = mul(shadow_delta, 1.0 / shadow_distance) if occluded(shadow_origin, shadow_direction, shadow_distance): continue # Uniform-area Monte Carlo estimate of the Lambertian area integral. weight = (LIGHT_AREA * cos_surface * cos_emitter / distance2 / (PI * light_samples)) for k in range(3): total[k] += albedo[k] * LIGHT_RADIANCE[k] * weight return tuple(total)
def camera_ray(x, y, width, height): origin = (0.0, 1.35, 4.55) forward = unit(sub((0.0, 0.72, 0.0), origin)) right = unit(cross(forward, (0.0, 1.0, 0.0))) up = unit(cross(right, forward)) aspect = width / height scale = math.tan(math.radians(48.0) / 2.0) sx = (2.0 * x / width - 1.0) * aspect * scale sy = (1.0 - 2.0 * y / height) * scale return origin, unit(add(forward, add(mul(right, sx), mul(up, sy))))
def linear_to_srgb(v): v = max(0.0, v) return 12.92 * v if v <= 0.0031308 else 1.055 * (v ** (1.0 / 2.4)) - 0.055
def render(width, height, spp, light_samples, seed): rng = random.Random(seed) pixels = bytearray() for y in range(height): for x in range(width): average = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for _ in range(spp): # Jittered primary rays supersample each pixel. origin, direction = camera_ray(x + rng.random(), y + rng.random(), width, height) hit = scene_hit(origin, direction) radiance = direct_radiance(hit[1], hit[2], hit[3], rng, light_samples) if hit else (0, 0, 0) for k in range(3): average[k] += radiance[k] / spp # Average in linear light, apply 2x Reinhard exposure, then encode sRGB. for value in average: exposed = 2.0 * value mapped = exposed / (1.0 + exposed) encoded = linear_to_srgb(mapped) if not math.isfinite(encoded): raise ArithmeticError("non-finite pixel") pixels.append(max(0, min(255, int(encoded * 255.0 + 0.5)))) return bytes(pixels)
def checks(): inside = sphere_hit((0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), ((0, 0, 0), 1, (1, 1, 1))) assert inside is not None and abs(inside[0] - 1.0) < 1e-9 # Exit root. ray = unit((0, -0.2, -1)) front = sphere_hit((0, 1, 3), ray, ((0, 0.7, 0), 0.5, (1, 1, 1))) floor = plane_hit((0, 1, 3), ray) assert front is not None and floor is not None and front[0] < floor[0] # Nearest hit. blocker = ((0, 0, 0), 0.4, (1, 1, 1)) SPHERES.append(blocker) assert not occluded((0, 0, 2), (0, 0, -1), 1.0) # Blocker beyond segment. assert occluded((0, 0, 2), (0, 0, -1), 3.0) # Same ray reaches blocker. SPHERES.pop() start, end = (0.1, 0.0, 2.0), (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) delta = sub(end, start); distance = length(delta); direction = unit(delta) assert length(sub(add(start, mul(direction, distance)), end)) < 1e-12 assert linear_to_srgb(0.0) == 0.0 and abs(linear_to_srgb(1.0) - 1.0) < 1e-12
def positive_int(value): result = int(value) if result < 1: raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError("must be a positive integer") return result
def main(): checks() parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__) parser.add_argument("--width", type=positive_int, default=96) parser.add_argument("--height", type=positive_int, default=64) parser.add_argument("--spp", type=positive_int, default=4, help="camera supersamples per pixel") parser.add_argument("--light-samples", type=positive_int, default=16) parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=178) parser.add_argument("--output", default="renderer-lab.ppm") args = parser.parse_args() payload = render(args.width, args.height, args.spp, args.light_samples, args.seed) assert len(payload) == args.width * args.height * 3 with open(args.output, "wb") as image: image.write(f"P6\n{args.width} {args.height}\n255\n".encode("ascii")) image.write(payload) print(f"wrote {args.output} ({args.width}x{args.height}, {args.spp} camera spp, {args.light_samples} light spp)")
if __name__ == "__main__": main()
Chapter.Content: XR systems closure — from a rendered eye image to a stable spatial computer

The earlier XR material establishes optics, perception, sampling, stereo geometry and foveation. The remaining system-level lesson is that XR is not a stereo renderer with a headset attached. It is a continuously estimated, predicted, calibrated, composited and human-observed closed loop. Every stage carries uncertainty, age, coordinate-frame meaning and a deadline.
XR is a spectrum of scene ownership

Virtual reality, augmented reality and mixed reality differ mainly in how much of the final view comes from reconstructed physical reality, how much comes from synthetic content, and who owns composition.

In fully synthetic VR the application may render nearly every visible surface, but the runtime still owns tracking interfaces, lens correction, composition and presentation timing. In optical see-through AR, real light reaches the eye directly, so virtual content must be aligned to a world the display cannot overwrite. In video see-through MR, cameras capture the physical world and a compositor combines that view with synthetic imagery. This gives stronger control over occlusion, exposure, color and depth-aware effects, but makes camera latency and reconstruction error part of the visible experience.

OpenXR formalizes an application-runtime boundary. The application supplies swapchain images and composition layers; the runtime owns device-facing details such as tracking integration, composition and final presentation. OpenXR 1.1 also promotes important ideas such as local-floor reference spaces and stereo foveated rendering into core functionality. An engine therefore should not encode one headset’s pose conventions deep inside gameplay.
Coordinate spaces are contracts about meaning and lifetime
A pose is not merely a position and quaternion. It is a transform from one named space to another at a specific time.

A useful XR system distinguishes view/head space, local or stage-like world spaces, floor-aligned spaces, action spaces attached to hands/controllers/gaze/tools, persistent anchors, and application world space. If a runtime reports a transform from B to A at time t, composition must preserve that meaning:
This notation prevents a destructive XR bug: multiplying matrices whose source and destination frames do not match.

Space lifetime matters. A local space can remain useful while global localization is weak. A persistent anchor can relocalize or be refined. A hand joint can disappear when confidence falls. Engine pose records therefore need validity, confidence and timestamp beside the transform rather than silently freezing the last good value.
The frame loop is organized around predicted display time

Desktop rendering is often summarized as update, render, present. XR requires a more precise timeline because the pose used for rendering should correspond to when photons from the frame reach the eye.
A runtime-oriented frame is conceptually:

ListItem.Content: wait for the runtime to schedule a frame;
receive the predicted display time;
locate views and action spaces for that future time;
simulate or interpolate application state;
render each requested view into runtime-provided swapchain images;
submit composition layers with their spaces and optional depth;
let the compositor perform late correction, lens processing and presentation.

Chapter.Content: The important quantity is the age of information at display, not CPU frame time alone. If gaze was sampled 12 ms ago, head pose was predicted for a different timestamp and the compositor presents later, visible error depends on the whole chain.

For orientation, prediction belongs on the rotation manifold:
Prediction helps only when its model error is smaller than the error from stale state. Abrupt motion can make aggressive prediction overshoot.
Reprojection corrects a finished frame; it does not rerender the world

The compositor may warp an already-rendered frame using a newer head pose. Rotational timewarp corrects orientation but cannot reveal correct disoccluded content and does not fix translational parallax. Positional reprojection can use submitted depth to approximate translation. Motion-aware methods can use motion vectors to extrapolate moving content.
Meta’s compositor documentation makes this hierarchy explicit: time warp updates head rotation; positional time warp uses depth for translation; App Spacewarp uses motion vectors for moving content.
Therefore:

ListItem.Content: orientation-only warp has no scene depth;
depth-aware warp inherits depth error;
motion-vector warp inherits velocity error;
no warp can reconstruct arbitrary newly visible geometry without additional information.

Chapter.Content: Black borders, stretched disocclusions, doubled edges and motion-vector disagreement are consequences of asking a warp to synthesize information absent from the source frame.
Optics make the pre-lens image intentionally distorted
The image written to a headset panel is often not a geometrically correct flat-monitor image. The lens warps rays, so the renderer or compositor applies an approximate inverse warp.
A simple radial model is

Real devices can use asymmetric, per-channel, mesh-based or proprietary calibration. Chromatic aberration exists because wavelengths refract differently, so one geometric warp need not align every color channel.

Runtime-provided view and projection data must therefore be treated as calibration data. Varjo’s OpenXR documentation illustrates this concretely: a headset may expose quad views, eye tracking, foveation, MR, depth submission and multiple composition layers through a combination of core and extensions.
Display timing is more than FPS
A headset display has refresh period, persistence, scanout behavior, brightness/contrast, pixel structure and optical MTF. If refresh rate is ,

At 90 Hz, one nominal refresh is about 11.11 ms, but motion-to-photon latency depends on tracking, queueing, rendering, compositor work and scanout. Reporting only 90 FPS hides the distribution that matters to head-coupled perception.
Tracking is state estimation under calibration and observability limits

An IMU provides high-rate angular velocity and specific force. Cameras provide visual constraints at lower rate. Integrating IMU bias causes drift; vision can fail under blur, low texture, repeated texture, extreme exposure or occlusion.
A visual-inertial state may contain

representing orientation, position, velocity and sensor biases. VIO propagates with inertial data and corrects with visual evidence. SLAM additionally maintains a map, loop closure and relocalization so old places can constrain drift.
Make the visual correction small enough to inspect: an eight-state planar EKF

The previous state list names orientation, position, velocity and sensor biases, but does not yet show how a camera observation changes them. Begin with a deliberately constrained model whose entire covariance update can be checked: a horizontal world plane, yaw-only rotation, gravity already removed from horizontal acceleration, and bearings to surveyed landmarks. This is an EKF witness for that model; it is not full 3-D VIO or SLAM.

For this experiment, the camera coordinate frame is known to coincide with the planar body frame : the optical center is at the body origin, camera forward is body , and the in-plane camera rotation is zero. Thus the fixed camera-to-body extrinsic , which maps camera coordinates into body coordinates, is , with zero lever arm and aligned axes. This is a stated identity-extrinsic assumption, not an estimated calibration result. The bearing equation below is valid because the camera and body origins and orientations coincide.
Use the state

where positions are metres, velocities are metres per second, yaw and gyro bias are radians and radians per second, and accelerometer biases are metres per second squared. Position and velocity are world-horizontal; accelerometer samples are body-horizontal. The rotation maps body vectors into world axes. Gyroscope measurement is ; specific-force measurement is . Here the simulation’s horizontal channel has gravity removed by construction.
For a zero-order hold over interval , subtract the estimated biases, rotate acceleration with the interval-start yaw, then integrate constant acceleration:
The transition Jacobian propagates uncertainty as . Sensor noise enters through a first-order map ; bias random walks add their variance per sample. A surveyed landmark gives camera bearing
For , , and , its nonzero Jacobian entries are , , and . As a hand check, at looking at , they are in radians per metre and radians per radian.

The wrapped innovation avoids treating bearings just across as almost a full revolution apart. With , reject a gross mismatch when exceeds the one-degree-of-freedom 99% chi-square threshold . Otherwise use , correct the state by , wrap yaw, and update covariance in Joseph form: . Joseph form better preserves symmetry and positive semidefiniteness under finite precision.

The complete source below fixes the clock at 50 Hz, uses three surveyed landmarks, injects one deliberately wrong correspondence, finite-differences every column of both analytic Jacobians, and checks covariance eigenvalues through a deterministic replay. Its 0.25 m final-position bound belongs only to this generated 4.8-second planar trajectory. It does not estimate camera intrinsics/extrinsics, time offset, roll/pitch, gravity direction, map structure, delayed observations, or human-head motion.
